hero.name: Geeta
hero.who: a 56-year-old homemaker in Varanasi who once loved writing poems and stopped

story.h: The poems in the steel trunk
story.b: Geeta lives near Assi Ghat in Varanasi with her husband, and her two children are now married and settled in Delhi. At nineteen, she filled three notebooks with Hindi poems. Then came marriage, children and school tiffins, and the notebooks went into a steel trunk under the bed. Now the house is quiet in the afternoons. Some days a line comes to her while she watches the boats on the river, and her heart jumps. But she never writes it down. Who would want to read an old woman's poems, she thinks, and anyway they would never be as good as the poets she studied in college. So the lines drift away like the river.

ask.q: Lines of poetry still come to Geeta, but she never writes them down. What is holding her back?
o: She is too old, and creative work belongs to young people
Fear and the need to be perfect, not a lack of ability
She has no time, with so many household duties
ask.why: Geeta has the time now and the lines keep arriving, so age and duties are not the real barriers. What stops her is fear of being judged and the belief that her work must match the great poets. Those fears can be faced, but only once she names them.

chapters.take: Often it is fear, not a lack of talent, that keeps creative work locked away.

story.b: Geeta does not feel ready to call herself a poet again. That word feels too heavy. But she notices a small curiosity. The old flower seller at the ghat hums songs Geeta half remembers from her own grandmother, songs women once sang while grinding grain. Geeta wonders where they came from. One morning she asks the flower seller about them, and the old woman laughs and sings a whole verse. Geeta writes it in a new notebook on the way home. The next day she asks her neighbour's mother. Fifteen minutes here, twenty there. She is not trying to be anything. She is just following a thread, and it keeps pulling her somewhere interesting.

ask.q: Geeta's daughter says she should set a big goal, like publishing a poetry book this year. What should Geeta do?
o: Accept the big goal, since only passion and pressure produce real work
Wait until she feels a strong passion before writing anything
Keep following her small curiosity about the old songs and see where it leads
ask.why: A huge goal can feel so heavy that she freezes, and waiting for passion may mean waiting forever. Curiosity is gentler. Following one small interest each day keeps her creating, and it often leads somewhere surprising, maybe even to a book one day.

chapters.take: You do not need a grand passion. Follow the small spark of curiosity.

story.b: The old songs start turning into poems of her own. Geeta's friend Sudha invites her to a small monthly poetry evening that a women's group holds in a community hall in Lanka. Geeta says no twice. On the third invitation she says yes, then lies awake all night. When her name is called, her hands shake so much the page rattles. Her voice cracks on the first line. She does not wait for the fear to leave. She lets it stand beside her and keeps reading, eight short lines about a grandmother's songs. When she looks up, two women in the front row are wiping their eyes. Her hands are still shaking as she sits down, and she is smiling.

ask.q: Geeta is terrified before her first poetry reading. What is the wisest way to handle the fear?
o: Let the fear be there and read anyway, even with shaking hands
Skip it and wait until the fear goes away completely
Read someone else's famous poem instead, so no one judges her work
ask.why: Fear tends to show up whenever we create, because creating means stepping into the unknown. Waiting for it to vanish can take forever, and reading a famous poem hides her own voice. Letting the fear come along while she acts is how her work finally gets heard.

chapters.take: Fear can come along for the ride. Just do not let it drive.

story.b: At a nephew's wedding in Prayagraj, word has spread about Geeta's poetry evening. A cousin's husband, a retired professor, raises his eyebrows over his plate of kachoris. He asks who exactly gave her the right to call herself a poet, without any degree in literature. A few relatives laugh. Geeta laughs too, but on the train home the question sits heavy in her chest. She even looks up a two-year literature diploma at the university, thinking maybe then she would be allowed. Then she looks at her notebook, now half full. Nobody gave the flower seller permission to sing. Geeta closes the university website and writes a new poem about the train window.

ask.q: A relative mocks Geeta for writing poems without a degree. What should she do?
o: Enrol in a two-year diploma first, so her poems are taken seriously
Keep writing, since she needs no one's permission to create
Stop sharing her poems with family to avoid embarrassment
ask.why: Nobody needs a certificate or approval to make things. Waiting for a diploma before writing turns a joy into an exam. Hiding her poems lets one sneering comment shrink her world. She is allowed to create simply because she wants to.

chapters.take: You do not need a degree or anyone's approval to make something.

story.b: Her son Rohan hears about the readings and gets excited. He sets up a video channel for her and says she could earn good money if she posts a poem every day. For three weeks Geeta tries. She checks the views each morning before her tea. A poem about her husband's snoring gets many views, and a quiet one about her mother gets very few. Soon she catches herself writing what might get clicks, not what she feels. The joy drains out. One afternoon she sits by the ghat with a blank page and feels dread for the first time. That evening she tells Rohan she will post only when she wants, and stops checking the numbers.

ask.q: Writing for views has made Geeta's poetry feel like a chore. What should she do?
o: Post even more often, since more videos will bring more money
Quit writing altogether, since it has stopped being fun
Free her poems from money pressure and write for the joy of it again
ask.why: Demanding that creative work pay can crush the playfulness that made it good. Posting more for money adds pressure, and quitting throws away something she loves. Letting her writing stay free of income goals brings back the curiosity and joy that started it.

chapters.take: Let your creative work be free to play. Not everything has to pay.

story.h: Forty poems and one stubborn line
story.b: By winter Geeta has forty poems in her notebook. She dreams of making a small booklet for her family. But every time she prepares to take it to the printer near Godowlia, she finds a line she wants to change. She has rewritten one poem eleven times. Weeks pass. Her granddaughter's first birthday is three weeks away, and Geeta realises the booklet could be her gift. She sees that waiting for perfect is just fear wearing a nicer sari. So she fixes a date, chooses twenty-five poems, leaves the stubborn line as it is and takes the pages to the printer. Fifty copies, with a simple cover showing the river.

ask.q: Geeta keeps rewriting her poems and the booklet never gets printed. What should she do?
o: Keep polishing until every line feels perfect, however long it takes
Set a date, choose her best poems and finish it, flaws and all
Drop the booklet idea and write only for herself
ask.why: Perfectionism often looks like high standards but works like fear, keeping work hidden forever. Setting a deadline and finishing lets the poems reach people who will love them. Endless polishing delays it again, and dropping the booklet lets fear win quietly.

chapters.take: Done and shared beats perfect and hidden. Finish it and let it go.

story.b: At the birthday lunch in Delhi, Geeta hands out her small booklets wrapped in newspaper and red thread. Her daughter reads one poem aloud and has to stop halfway. Even the professor cousin asks for a copy, a little stiffly. Back in Varanasi, Geeta keeps writing most afternoons, following whatever catches her eye: a boatman's song, a goat on the steps, the smell of rain on old stone. She still reads at the monthly evening in Lanka, and her hands still tremble a little. The channel gets a new poem only when she feels like it. She has already started a second notebook, and this one is not going into the trunk.

chapters.take: Creativity grows when you follow curiosity, face fear and keep sharing your work.
